Analysis v10: Core Evidence Package — Leapfrogging

Oxford University Ledgers, 1700–1900. Restructured around advisor feedback (2026-05-26): focused core evidence for leapfrogging story; secondary findings preserved in companion research inventory.

Central claim: Institutional shocks (1854 & 1877 Reform Acts) triggered leapfrogging toward higher-order transformation — capability expansion (L3) and mission redefinition (L4) — before lower-order operational optimisation (efficiency L1, process L2) was completed. The Reform Acts function as strategic discontinuities rather than gradual modernisation triggers.
What's essential vs supporting: Figures marked ESSENTIAL carry the leapfrogging argument and belong in the manuscript. Figures marked SUPPORTING add texture but can be moved to appendix or dropped without weakening the core claim. The Strength assessment at the bottom maps each sub-claim to its quantitative basis.

1. Framework: Four Dimensions of Transformation

The four-level framework is treated as dimensions of transformation, not deterministic stages. The empirical question is which dimensions activate first, and under what institutional conditions.

2. The Leapfrogging Mechanism (Core Evidence)

Mechanism in one sentence: Higher-order dimensions (L3 capability, L4 mission) exhibit disproportionately larger responses to institutional shocks than lower-order dimensions (L1 efficiency, L2 process). Three quantitative angles below — normalised trajectories, normalised ITS effects, and break magnitudes.

2.1 Normalised Growth Trajectories

Each level rescaled to its 1820–1853 pre-reform mean (= 1). If transformation were uniform across dimensions, all four trajectories would diverge similarly. The visible divergence — L4 rising multiple-fold while L1/L2 stay near baseline — is the leapfrogging signature.

Interrupted time-series level-shift coefficients at each Reform Act, divided by each level's own pre-reform mean. Removes scale differences so levels can be compared directly.

3. Reform Acts as Strategic Discontinuities

Two complementary tests of whether the 1854 reform was a discontinuous jump or just a phase of fast linear change. Both reject the gradual-drift interpretation.

3.1 Signal-to-Noise of Breaks

Break magnitude at 1854 divided by the pre-reform rolling standard deviation (10-year window average). High ratio = sharp shift relative to typical year-to-year noise.

3.2 Sharpness Index

Fraction of total post-1854 level gain that occurs within the first 5 years. Under a linear trend, this fraction should equal 5/n_post_years (~0.135). Observed values 6–10× larger ⇒ change concentrated immediately post-reform, not spread evenly.

6. Paper Skeleton (Leapfrogging-Centred)

6.1 Research question

Do organisations facing major institutional shocks transform through a predictable operational-first sequence, or do they leapfrog directly into higher-order capability and mission transformation? Using 200 years of Oxford University accounting ledgers (1700–1900), we ask whether external reforms can short-circuit the efficiency-then-redesign sequence assumed in many technology-adoption models.

6.2 Theoretical motivation

  • Punctuated equilibrium: institutional shocks may trigger simultaneous multi-dimensional reorganisation, bypassing lower-order stages.
  • Resource-based view + slack: endowment-funded organisations may have the financial capacity to leapfrog; fiscally-constrained organisations may not.
  • AI analogy: contemporary firms investing in AI talent and org redesign before optimising operations may be rationally responding to external pressure rather than aberrantly skipping stages.

6.3 Data & identification

  • 1,581 scanned ledger pages, annual panel of real-£ expenditure shares by category.
  • Treatment: 1854 University Reform Act and 1877 University of Oxford Act (exogenous parliamentary timing).
  • Identification: interrupted time series (ITS) with HAC standard errors; structural-break detection (binseg); signal-to-noise and sharpness tests for the discontinuous-vs-gradual distinction.

6.4 Main finding

Reform Acts function as strategic discontinuities that produce disproportionately large responses in higher-order dimensions (L3 capability, L4 mission) relative to lower-order dimensions (L1 efficiency, L2 process). At the 1877 reform, L4's normalised effect is 2.41× pre-reform mean — roughly 60× larger than L1. L4's relative break magnitude (3.63×) is an order of magnitude larger than L2 (0.06×). The 1854 reform shows the same asymmetry in disruption: L3/L4 hit hardest in absolute terms, L1/L2 barely move.

6.5 Mechanism

External institutional pressure forces rapid capability investment (salary growth, new appointments) and mission redefinition (educational expansion) before the organisation can fully articulate a new strategic plan. Endowment-funded resource slack (from rising land rents) provides the financial capacity to leapfrog; organisations under fiscal constraint cannot. The leapfrogging of L1/L2 suggests external shocks can short-circuit the efficiency-then-redesign sequence typically assumed in technology adoption models.

6.6 Contemporary AI parallel

Firms investing in AI capability and org redesign ahead of operational optimisation may be following the same shock-driven leapfrogging pattern Oxford exhibited under the Reform Acts. Regulatory mandates around AI may function analogously to the 19th-century Reform Acts — forcing higher-order transformation first.

6.7 Boundary conditions

  • Transformation pace (200 years) is pre-industrial — not generalisable to AI tempo.
  • Oxford's no-competition / endowment-funded structure is unusual; analogy is to well-capitalised firms with retained earnings, not to all firms.
  • Mechanism (shock-driven leapfrogging) is the generalisable contribution, not the pace.
